content: 1. Currently, there is no evidence to confirm that individuals who have recovered from COVID-19 and have detectable antibodies in their blood are immune or protected from reinfection. 2. The first documented case of COVID-19 reinfection occurred on August 15, 2020, involving a man in Hong Kong who tested positive again four and a half months after his initial infection. The second infection was caused by a different strain of the virus. 3. There is no evidence to suggest that reinfection with COVID-19 is more severe than the initial infection. 4. Individuals who are reinfected with COVID-19 are likely to experience symptoms similar to those of their initial infection. 5. It is currently unknown whether the presence of low concentrations of viral RNA after clinical recovery indicates the presence of infectious virus. Based on experience with other viruses, it is unlikely that such individuals pose an infectious risk to others. However, this has not been definitively established for SARS-CoV-2. 6. After the onset of illness, the detectable viral burden typically declines. Within a week or more, anti-SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulins become detectable, and antibody titers increase. Some of these antibodies may neutralize the virus in cell culture. The decline in viral burden is associated with a reduced ability to isolate live virus. 7. Efforts to isolate live virus from upper respiratory tract specimens have been unsuccessful when samples are collected more than 10 days after the onset of illness. 8. Individuals who test persistently or recurrently positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA have shown stable or improving clinical signs of illness. Attempts to isolate live virus from such individuals in South Korea and the United States have been unsuccessful. 9. There is no evidence that clinically recovered individuals with persistent or recurrent detection of viral RNA have transmitted COVID-19 to others. 10. Despite encouraging observations, it cannot be conclusively stated that individuals with persistent or recurrent detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA are no longer infectious. 11. There is no definitive evidence that antibodies developed in response to infection are protective. If they are protective, the antibody titers required for protection against reinfection are unknown. 12. Based on available data and experience with other viral infections, most individuals recovered from COVID-19 who test persistently or recurrently positive by RT-PCR are likely no longer infectious. 13. The magnitude and persistence of the immune response following recovery may vary among individuals, with factors such as age potentially influencing the level of protection. 14. Decisions regarding whether recovered individuals with persistently detectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA are potentially infectious and should remain in isolation must be made on a case-by-case basis. This determination should consider factors such as medical history, time since the initial positive test, RT-PCR cycle threshold (Ct) values, and the presence of COVID-19 signs or symptoms. 15. To confirm that persistent or recurrent shedding of SARS-CoV-2 RNA after recovery does not represent the presence of infectious virus, it is necessary to prospectively collect serial respiratory samples and attempt to isolate live virus in tissue culture from multiple individuals testing positive by RT-PCR after clinical recovery. If repeated attempts to recover replication-competent virus in culture from such samples are unsuccessful, this would provide sufficient evidence that infectious virus is absent and that these individuals do not pose an infectious risk to others. 16. If an individual has clinically recovered using a symptom-based strategy, they do not need a test to confirm that they are no longer infectious. The symptom-based strategy is intended to replace repeat testing. 17. Many recovered individuals do not have detectable SARS-CoV-2 RNA in upper respiratory tract specimens. In others, viral RNA can persistently be detected by RT-PCR in respiratory tract samples after clinical recovery. 18. In some individuals, after testing negative by RT-PCR in two consecutive samples, later samples may test positive again. These later samples often contain fewer RNA copies than earlier samples collected during clinical illness. 19. Studies have shown that SARS-CoV-2 RNA can be detected in some individuals for weeks after recovery. 20. Cycle threshold (Ct) values cannot be used to determine when a person is no longer infectious. Although attempts to culture virus from upper respiratory specimens have largely been unsuccessful when Ct values are high but detectable, Ct values are not a quantitative measure of viral burden. Ct values are not standardized across RT-PCR platforms and have not been approved by the FDA for clinical management. The CDC does not endorse or recommend the use of Ct values to assess infectiousness. However, serial Ct values may be useful when considered alongside other clinical information to assess recovery and resolution of infection. 21. Even after clinical recovery, individuals should continue to wear masks in public. It is recommended that all individuals, with a few exceptions, wear cloth face coverings in public settings. 22. The primary purpose of cloth face coverings is to limit the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 from infected individuals who may be infectious but asymptomatic or have mild symptoms they do not recognize. Cloth face coverings may also provide reassurance to others in public settings and serve as a reminder to maintain social distancing. 23. Cloth face coverings are not personal protective equipment (PPE) and should not be used as a substitute for respirators or face masks to protect healthcare workers. 24. Cloth face coverings should not be placed on young children under the age of 2, anyone who has trouble breathing, or anyone who is unconscious, incapacitated, or otherwise unable to remove the mask without assistance. 25. Within three months of recovery, a person who has clinically recovered from COVID-19 and is later identified as a contact of a new case does not need to be quarantined or retested for SARS-CoV-2. 26. After three months, if a person is identified as a contact of a new case, they should follow quarantine recommendations for contacts.
